title: He Wants AI Benchmarking To Be a Science, Not a Dark Art
content:
Moritz Hardt, author of a new book on benchmarks, believes these “standardized tests” for artificial intelligence are fundamentally broken — but not unfixable.

![Image 1: Man sitting on a green couch.](https://www.quantamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Moritz-Hardt-QA-cr.Jerrit-Peinelt-Lede-scaled.webp)

The computer scientist Moritz Hardt calls benchmarks “the mistake that made machine learning.” He’s studied where they went wrong, and why they’ve managed to drive progress anyway.

Jerrit Peinelt for _Quanta Magazine_

## Introduction

Benchmarks are the rulers of AI, in both senses of the word. As measuring sticks, they work according to an extremely simple logic: If you want to know what an AI model can do, devise a standardized test to gauge it. But AI benchmarks can also dominate the behavior of the entire field.

In 1987, the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency’s [first benchmark (opens a new tab)](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.06647v1#S5) on automatic speech-to-text translation showed that state-of-the-art AI could not outperform so-called “dumb” statistical approaches. The poor performance helped to usher in an AI winter. For 25 years, interest in AI research waned and funding dried up.

Then, in 2012, [another benchmark (opens a new tab)](https://www.image-net.org/challenges/LSVRC/index.php) called ImageNet swung the pendulum back. An eight-layer neural network [trounced (opens a new tab)](https://spectrum.ieee.org/alexnet-source-code) other algorithms at classifying images and kicked off a “deep learning revolution.”

Nowadays, new AI benchmarks, geared at large language models such as OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra, get created and solved with clockwork regularity, purporting to measure everything from [domain-specific expertise (opens a new tab)](https://hai.stanford.edu/ai-index/2026-ai-index-report/technical-performance) to “[general intelligence (opens a new tab)](https://arcprize.org/arc-agi).” But rather than hail this trend as proof of AI’s skyrocketing potential, many in the field — [skeptics (opens a new tab)](https://x.com/GaryMarcus/status/2028488127875342724) and [boosters (opens a new tab)](https://x.com/karpathy/status/1896266683301659068?lang=en) alike — take it as evidence that benchmarking itself has become [fatally flawed (opens a new tab)](https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-025-02462-5).

[Moritz Hardt (opens a new tab)](https://mrtz.org/), a computer scientist and a director at the Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems, agrees with this diagnosis. Shortly after the ImageNet result, he began to think that machine learning systems could game leaderboards “without doing anything intelligent.” “There’s no two ways about it,” he said. “The benchmarking ecosystem is broken.”

In his 2026 book [_The Emerging Science of Machine Learning Benchmarks_ (opens a new tab)](https://mlbenchmarks.org/), Hardt makes the provocative case that these measuring sticks have been broken for decades already: Benchmarks, he writes, are “the mistake that made machine learning.” Notably, he argues, instead of creating a replicability crisis, they drove legitimate progress anyway — “mostly by sheer luck,” in his view. By understanding why, we can explain how benchmarks have since lost this accidental credibility in the age of LLMs, and how they might regain it.

_Quanta_ spoke to Hardt about what went wrong, and right, with benchmarks, and where to take them next. The interview has been condensed and edited for clarity.

![Image 2: Man in profile, sitting at his computer.](https://www.quantamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Moritz-Hardt-QA-cr.Jerrit-Peinelt-Sitting-profile-scaled.webp)

Hardt is fascinated by how benchmarks paradoxically helped start both a 25-year AI winter in the late 1980s and a deep learning revolution in the 2010s.

Jerrit Peinelt for _Quanta Magazine_

### **Let’s get the basics straight: What even is a benchmark?**

The recipe is simple. To evaluate a machine learning model, you take your data and split it into a training set and a test set. You let the model builders do whatever they want on the training set: Anything goes, no rules. But you use the test set only to compare and rank models — to have a leaderboard say, “This is currently state-of-the-art, this is number one, this is number two.”

### **So a benchmark for a large language model today, like GPT-6 Astra or Claude Fable, might test an ability to**[**solve difficult math problems** (opens a new tab)](https://epoch.ai/frontiermath)**or**[**find security bugs in software** (opens a new tab)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.14153)**.**

Right. The first benchmark, in fact, was created in 1959. It was a set of digits and letters printed on punch cards, meant to test how well different scanners could [recognize written characters (opens a new tab)](https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/optical-character-recognition). Somebody introduced the train-test split and started a leaderboard.

It wasn’t like there was some master plan. But that’s what we now call benchmarking, and it’s been the engine of progress in AI for about 60 years or so.

### **What are benchmarks supposed to tell us?**

Traditionally, a benchmark is supposed to be like a thermometer. People train a model to do something, and then you come up with some kind of measurement procedure to see how good the model is.

But in practice, benchmarking is more like a sports competition or a market. Benchmarks define the rules of the game, and people actively compete over them, and we let the best model win.

![Image 3: Man in a purple jacket sitting outdoors.](https://www.quantamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Moritz-Hardt-QA-cr.Jerrit-Peinelt-With-tree-scaled.webp)

Hardt cautions that the scores AI models receive on benchmarks don’t mean much. But comparisons, or rankings, among models do.

Jerrit Peinelt for _Quanta Magazine_

### **Can’t they be both? What’s the problem?**

Any machine learning textbook will tell you about the “holdout method” — that you should lock away the test set, and only use it once to rank the models. If you ignore this, you’re on thin ice. You might get very misleading results because you’re evaluating models that in some sense have knowledge of the test set.

The fascinating thing is that machine learning as a discipline just ignored the warning. It took all these test sets and put them on the internet for everyone to use. It’s easy to put these test sets in a model’s development loop and to keep iterating on them.

### **Is that what’s “broken” about benchmarks?**

If you look at a model’s accuracy numbers on one benchmark, and then you change the test set only slightly, you get completely different accuracy numbers. That’s the sense in which the benchmark is not working. If you have 90% accuracy on one dataset and 73% on another, which is it? I have no idea how good this model is.

### **OpenAI, Anthropic, and other technology companies still advertise benchmark numbers as a measurement of their models’ reasoning capabilities. Is that just nonsense?**

These scores really get misused. If you say, “On this math benchmark, the model got a 90%, which means that the model is now equivalent to an expert mathematician,” you’re reading something into that number that gives you the wrong takeaway. We should avoid comparisons or conclusions that implicitly require the absolute number to make sense.

![Image 4: Man sitting at his desk in front of a whiteboard.](https://www.quantamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Moritz-Hardt-QA-cr.Jerrit-Peinelt-Computer-scaled.webp)

“There’s something sad to the triumph of benchmarking, because it seems like we’re giving up what science is actually about: understanding the mechanisms,” Hardt said. “But benchmarking can, in the long run, lead to new scientific knowledge.”

Jerrit Peinelt for _Quanta Magazine_

### **If the absolute numbers don’t make sense, how do you not end up with a replication crisis?**

This is where things get really interesting. If, instead of absolute numbers, you look at rankings — relative comparisons between models — those rankings tend to be very stable across different datasets. And this has been pretty consistent across the history of machine learning. If one model gets 90% on a particular test set, and another model gets 80%, then the 90% model is the model you’d want to use in the real world. It’ll still do better on other datasets, even ones that are quite different than the test set.

That, to me, is the main reason why machine learning escaped a scientific crisis.

### **That’s surprising. So the 90% score doesn’t have much validity, but the fact that it “won” the competition does?**

Yeah. So benchmarks tell you when you beat the previous best. And these improvement indicators are pretty reliable.

But it’s lucky that it worked as well as it did — we had no reason to expect this to be the case. And we don’t yet have a good comprehensive theory for why this happens. It’s mostly an empirical phenomenon.

### **But you also argue that now, in the era of large language models, benchmarks are no longer able to deliver this “accidental” reliability. Why not?**

The stability of model rankings has one big caveat: Models need to train on the same training set. In the old days, this was always true. But we don’t know what LLMs were trained on. In fact, model builders can strategically assemble data mixes that best promote benchmark performance. It’s a little bit like studying to the test, which we all do in high school.

That’s why we’re currently in this benchmarking crisis — because it’s no longer true that the better model necessarily wins. A worse model might just put more effort into preparing for the specific benchmark.

This isn’t really a crime: It happens every time a new model is released. If you look at the notes on the latest version of Gemini or GPT, you’ll see that its performance on benchmarks that were released before the new model is often fantastic, while its performance on benchmarks released shortly after is way lower. That’s always an indication that the model was “post-trained” on the earlier benchmark — what some people call “benchmaxxed.” And it’s generally accepted.

![Image 5: Man standing outside, leaning against a railing.](https://www.quantamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Moritz-Hardt-QA-cr.Jerrit-Peinelt-Balcony-scaled.webp)

Hardt says that AI models should receive “altitude training” for benchmarks.

Jerrit Peinelt for _Quanta Magazine_

### **Is there a way out of this benchmarking crisis, as you call it?**

Let me tell you a story: At the 1968 Olympics in Mexico City, there was an American runner who was vastly favored to win the 1,500-meter race. He [lost unexpectedly to a runner (opens a new tab)](https://www.runnersworld.com/uk/training/motivation/a34396756/kip-keino-1968/) from the Kenyan highlands, by a wide margin. The Kenyan runner had trained at high elevation and was better prepared for competing at 7,500 feet above sea level. It caused some controversy: Should we outlaw altitude training? The consensus in the end was, just let everyone do it.

The problem is not so much that people optimize to the benchmarks — it’s that they optimize to different degrees. If everyone optimizes, or “altitude trains,” the absolute numbers will be inflated, but you can restore the validity of the rankings.

### **What would altitude training for AI benchmarks look like?**

We don’t know ahead of time what went into these models, but we can train them for a little bit on benchmark-relevant data, just to make sure that we’re leveling the playing field somewhat.

In this new view of benchmarks, you would have no training set. You would have a test set, and you would also have some kind of protocol for preparing each of the models before you test them — that’s the altitude training.

### **But even if this works, we’re just back to where we started: progress indicators, but no valid measurements. Without that, how can we learn anything about how the models work?**

This is a really interesting question. There’s something sad to the triumph of benchmarking, because it seems like we’re giving up what science is actually about: understanding the mechanisms. But if we had some kind of grand mathematical theory to build these models with, we wouldn’t need the benchmarks.

We don’t know how these models do it, and benchmarking won’t tell us.

But benchmarking can, in the long run, lead to new scientific knowledge. The [CASP protein-folding benchmark](https://www.quantamagazine.org/how-ai-revolutionized-protein-science-but-didnt-end-it-20240626/) advanced science without first insisting on a scientific theory of protein folding. That’s the paradoxical power of benchmarking in the sciences.

# Bruce Springsteen on Surviving Depression and His Strategy for Living Through the Visitations of the Darkness

### By Maria Popova

[![Image 35: Bruce Springsteen on Surviving Depression and His Strategy for Living Through the Visitations of the Darkness](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/07/brucespringsteen_borntorun.jpg?fit=320%2C468&ssl=1)](https://www.amazon.com/Born-Run-Bruce-Springsteen/dp/1501141511/?tag=braipick-20)

It starts with a low hum that adheres itself to the underbelly of the hours like another dimension. Gradually, surreptitiously, the noise swells to a bellowing bass line, until it drowns out the symphony of life.

It can last for days or months or entire seasons of being. It visited Keats frequently in his short life, leaving him [with a mind empty of ideas and hands heavy as lead](https://www.themarginalian.org/2019/06/13/keats-depression/). It rendered Lorraine Hansberry [“cold, useless, frustrated, helpless, disillusioned, angry and tired.”](https://www.themarginalian.org/2019/10/07/lorraine-hansberry-depression/) It drove Abraham Lincoln [to the brink of suicide](https://www.themarginalian.org/2020/12/03/lincoln-melancholy-depression/).

If you are lucky enough, if you have the right aids of science, social support, and chance, one day you look over the shoulder of time and, like the poet Jane Kenyon, gasp in grateful incomprehension: [“What hurt me so terribly all my life until this moment?”](https://www.themarginalian.org/2017/09/27/having-it-out-with-melancholy-jane-kenyon-amanda-palmer/) But until that moment comes, as William Styron so vividly observed in his [classic bridge of empathy](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/02/09/depression-william-styron-darkness-visible/), “the gray drizzle of horror induced by depression takes on the quality of physical pain.”

Among the legion of us soaked by the drizzle is one of the most beloved artists of our epoch, whose music has made life brighter and more livable for generations.

[![Image 36](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/07/brucespringsteen_driving.jpg?resize=680%2C454&ssl=1)](https://www.amazon.com/Born-Run-Bruce-Springsteen/dp/1501141511/?tag=braipick-20)

Bruce Springsteen driving cross-country in 1987. (Photograph from [_Born to Run_](https://www.amazon.com/Born-Run-Bruce-Springsteen/dp/1501141511/?tag=braipick-20).)

In his memoir, [**_Born to Run_**](https://www.amazon.com/Born-Run-Bruce-Springsteen/dp/1501141511/?tag=braipick-20) ([_public library_](https://www.worldcat.org/title/born-to-run/oclc/1026404147&referer=brief_results)), **Bruce Springsteen** writes about his father’s “long, drawn-out depressions,” often so debilitating that he could not rise from bed for days, and about his own tumble toward the edge of the abyss quarried by his genetic inheritance and the darknesses of his childhood, and about what kept him from falling. “God help Bruce Springsteen when they decide he’s no longer God,” John Lennon reflected in [his most personal interview](https://www.themarginalian.org/2022/02/16/john-lennon-jonathan-cott-interview/), but no outside “they” — no critic, no cry from the public — ever measures up to the inner chorus of anguish that most cruelly lowers an artist from the pedestal of their creative power and into the pit of depression.

In a particularly vivid vignette from the period just before he finally sought help, Springsteen writes:

> My depression is spewing like an oil spill all over the beautiful turquoise-green gulf of my carefully planned and controlled existence. Its black sludge is threatening to smother every last living part of me.

Even [Springsteen’s favorite books](https://www.themarginalian.org/2014/11/03/bruce-springsteen-reading-list-favorite-books/) reflect this lifelong undertone of black. But it is in his [BBC _Desert Island Discs_](https://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/articles/9FNJXs9HzJhV6jZ4rMCKN3/which-eight-songs-would-bruce-springsteen-take-to-a-desert-island) appearance that he opens up most candidly about his experience of depression and his life-honed coping mechanisms for it. He reflects:

> I’ve developed some skills that help me in dealing with it, but still — it is a powerful, powerful thing that really comes up from things that still remain unexplainable to me.

![Image 37](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/07/BruceSpringsteen_BBC.jpg?resize=680%2C383&ssl=1)

Bruce Springsteen. (Photograph: BBC.)

After noting that much of it is pure biochemistry, and can therefore be greatly salved by biochemical interventions, he considers the psychological skills that have helped him temper the onslaught and offers a Buddhist-like strategy of unresistant presence with the flow of experience on its own terms, laced with a gentle admonition against the trap of blamethirsty projection:

> Just naming it [helps]… What most people tend to want to do is, when they feel bad, the first thing you want to do is to name a reason why you feel that way: “I feel bad because…” and you’ll transfer that to someone else “…because Johnny said this to me,” or “this happened.” And, sometimes, that’s true. But a lot of times, you’re simply looking to name something that’s not particularly nameable and if you misname it, it just makes everything that much worse.
> 
> 
> So my “skill” is sort of saying, “Okay, it’s not this, it’s not that — it’s just _this_. This is something that comes; it’s also something that goes — and maybe something I have to live with for a period of time.”
> 
> 
> But if you can acknowledge it and you can relax with it a little bit, very often it shortens its duration.

Complement with [_Bloom_](https://www.themarginalian.org/2020/02/27/bloom-depression/) — a touching animated short film about depression and what it takes to recover the light of being — and Tim Ferriss on [how he survived his suicidal depression](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/12/08/tim-ferriss-tools-of-titans-depression/), then revisit Robert Burton’s centuries-old [salve for melancholy](https://www.themarginalian.org/2022/01/18/robert-burton-melancholy-body-mind/) and two centuries of beloved writers — including Keats, Whitman, Hansberry, Carson, and Thoreau — on [the mightiest antidote to depression](https://www.themarginalian.org/2020/06/14/nature-depression/).
